title: A New Clue to the Puzzle of the Expanding Universe
summary:
Scientists know the universe is expanding, but they disagree about how fast. Two of the best ways to measure the speed, called the Hubble constant, give answers that do not match. This puzzle is known as the Hubble tension.

One method uses the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang. Telescopes such as the Planck Space Telescope measured tiny patterns in this ancient light. Using a model of the universe, those patterns predict an expansion rate of about 67 kilometers per second per megaparsec.

The second method is more direct. It measures how fast faraway galaxies move away from us, using the brightness of exploding stars called supernovae. Because these supernovae have a known brightness, how dim they look shows how far away they are. Observations with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes give a higher value of about 73. The difference may seem small, but it is statistically very significant. If both methods are correct, the standard model of the universe may be missing something.

A team of researchers wondered whether tiny magnetic fields from the very early universe could help. Scientists have studied these "primordial" fields for years. The team's idea is that such fields would have changed how the first hydrogen formed, making matter slightly clumpy. That would shift the moment the universe became transparent. It would also change the "cosmic ruler" used to measure distances, which could ease the tension.

For the first time, the team ran full three-dimensional simulations of the early universe with magnetic fields and tested the results against observations. Their idea remained possible. They found a mild preference for these fields, which they say is not yet a discovery, but a meaningful hint.
why_it_matters: If both measurements are right, the standard model of the universe must be missing something important, so a new idea like this could lead to better understanding.
